title: Why the Prompt Is a Design Surface
content:
In an AI product, the system prompt determines the voice, the format, the tone, the confidence language, the refusal behaviour, and the length of everything the user reads. That is design work, written in prose, usually by an engineer, usually without a designer in the room.

WHAT LIVES IN THE PROMPT THAT IS UNAMBIGUOUSLY DESIGN:
- Voice and tone, including per-state tone (ab-002).
- Output format and structure — which is layout, expressed as a constraint.
- Length. The most common quality complaint about AI output and a pure design decision.
- Confidence language and hedging policy (at-002).
- Refusal wording and boundary framing (at-004).
- Error and correction behaviour (ab-003).
- What the system offers unprompted, and what it stays quiet about.

THE PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE: if you are designing an AI feature and have not read its system prompt, you have not seen the design. Ask for it, read it, and expect to find decisions you would have made differently — usually verbosity, usually excessive hedging, usually a persona assembled from adjectives.

HOW TO CONTRIBUTE WITHOUT BECOMING A PROMPT ENGINEER:
- Write the examples. Three good outputs and three bad ones for each task type is the most useful artefact you can hand over, and it is a design deliverable in the same category as a component spec.
- Specify the output CONTRACT — shape, maximum length, required and forbidden elements — rather than trying to write the prose that produces it.
- Own the evaluation rubric (ab-006). If design owns the definition of good, design owns the quality bar.
- Review prompt changes the way you would review a component change, because their effect on the interface is comparable.

title: System Prompt Structure
content:
A workable order, most stable to most variable:

1. ROLE AND PURPOSE. One or two sentences. What this system is and what it is for.
2. AUDIENCE AND CONTEXT. Who is on the other side and what they are trying to do.
3. BEHAVIOURAL RULES. What it must always do, what it must never do. Ordered by priority so conflicts resolve predictably.
4. VOICE AND TONE. Concrete and behavioural, not adjectival (ab-001).
5. OUTPUT FORMAT. The contract — shape, length limits, required elements, forbidden elements.
6. CAPABILITIES AND BOUNDARIES. What it can do, what it cannot, and how to say so.
7. EDGE-CASE HANDLING. Not knowing, being corrected, refusing, the user being distressed.
8. EXAMPLES. Few-shot demonstrations of the hard cases.
9. DYNAMIC CONTEXT. User data, retrieved documents, session state — last, and clearly delimited.

PRINCIPLES:
- POSITIVE INSTRUCTIONS BEAT PROHIBITIONS. 'Answer in one paragraph, then offer detail' works better than 'don't be verbose'.
- SPECIFICITY IS EVERYTHING. 'Concise' is unenforceable; 'at most three sentences unless the user asks for more' is checkable.
- ORDER RULES BY PRIORITY and say what wins when they conflict. Unresolved conflicts produce inconsistency, which is the thing you were trying to prevent.
- DELIMIT DYNAMIC CONTENT clearly, so retrieved content cannot be read as instruction. This is a security boundary, not a formatting nicety.
- EXAMPLES OVER DESCRIPTION for anything about format or tone. Two examples outperform a paragraph reliably.
- KEEP IT AS SHORT AS IT CAN BE. Long prompts dilute; instructions at the back get less weight than instructions at the front.

WHAT TO TEST AFTER EVERY EDIT: the fixed regression set (ab-004). Prompt changes have non-local effects, and the failure you introduce is rarely in the area you edited.

title: Constraint Specification — Making 'Good' Enforceable
content:
Vague instruction produces variable output. Constraints are how you make the output contract real.

THE CONSTRAINT TYPES, and how to write each:
- LENGTH. Give a number and a unit. 'At most 3 sentences', 'under 150 words', 'exactly 5 bullets'. 'Brief' is not a constraint.
- STRUCTURE. Name the shape. 'A one-line answer, then up to three supporting bullets, then nothing.' Better still, a schema.
- VOCABULARY. Required terms (matching your UI labels), and banned terms — jargon, marketing language, 'I'm 100% sure', 'always', 'never' without justification.
- FORMAT. Markdown or plain, headers permitted or not, code fences, table shape, emoji policy.
- SCOPE. What to include and what to leave out. 'Do not restate the question.' 'Do not offer further help at the end.'
- ORDER. 'Answer first, then reasoning.' This single constraint improves perceived quality more than most others, because it stops preamble.
- CONFIDENCE. Which hedging language is permitted at which confidence level (at-002).

WRITING THEM WELL:
- Positive and specific over negative and vague.
- One constraint per line, so a violation is attributable.
- Say what wins when constraints conflict. Length versus completeness will conflict; decide in advance which one yields.
- Make them checkable. A constraint you cannot verify automatically cannot be regression-tested, and will drift.

THE HIGHEST-VALUE CONSTRAINTS IN PRACTICE, in order: answer-before-explanation, a hard length ceiling, no closing offer of further help, and no preamble. Those four remove most of what makes AI output tiring to read, and all four are design decisions.

title: Examples and Few-Shot Patterns
content:
Examples are the most reliable instrument you have for controlling format and tone, and the easiest for a designer to produce.

WHAT MAKES A GOOD EXAMPLE SET:
- COVERS THE HARD CASES, not the easy ones. The system handles the straightforward request already. Show it the ambiguous request, the out-of-scope request, the request where the answer is 'it depends', and the request where the correct response is a question.
- PAIRED GOOD AND BAD. For each case, the approved response and a rejected one, with a one-line note on why. The contrast teaches more than the positive example alone.
- CONSISTENT INTERNALLY. If your examples vary in format, you have specified variation.
- REPRESENTATIVE IN LENGTH. Examples are copied in shape, including their length. Long examples produce long output.
- ORDERED with the most typical case last, since recency carries weight.

HOW MANY: three to five per task type is the usual sweet spot. Beyond that you are spending context for diminishing returns, and the examples start to conflict.

THE DESIGNER'S VERSION OF THIS ARTEFACT: a table with columns for user input, approved response, rejected response, and the reason. It doubles as the persona specification, the evaluation set, and the regression suite. It is the single most leveraged document a designer can contribute to an AI product, and it requires no engineering skill to produce.

PITFALLS:
- Examples that encode an assumption you did not intend — all example users being one persona, all examples in one register, all questions being well-formed.
- Examples that become stale after a model or prompt change and are never re-reviewed.
- Using real user data as examples without consent.

title: Context Engineering — What to Put in the Window
content:
Context is a budget. Spending it well is the difference between a reliable feature and an erratic one.

WHAT COMPETES FOR IT: the system prompt, examples, conversation history, retrieved documents, tool definitions and outputs, and the user's current input.

PRINCIPLES:
- RELEVANCE OVER VOLUME. More retrieved context frequently makes output worse, not better, because the signal is diluted. Retrieve narrowly and precisely.
- POSITION MATTERS. Instructions at the beginning and the end get more weight than instructions in the middle. Put the output contract at both ends if it keeps being violated.
- DELIMIT EVERYTHING that came from outside. Retrieved content, user files, and tool output must be visibly bounded so they cannot be read as instruction. This is prompt-injection defence and it is structural, not optional.
- SUMMARISE HISTORY DELIBERATELY. When a conversation exceeds the window, what gets dropped is a design decision. Established constraints and stated preferences should survive; small talk should not.
- SAY WHEN CONTEXT IS DROPPED (ax-007). A user whose earlier constraint is silently forgotten experiences unreliability, not a technical limit.

THE UX CONSEQUENCES THAT DESIGN OWNS:
- What the user can see about current scope, and what they can add or remove.
- Whether scope is manipulable as objects (chips, file pills) or buried in a settings panel.
- Whether persistent memory exists, and whether it is inspectable and deletable.
- What happens at the boundary — a warning, a summary, a forced new session, or silent degradation. Silent degradation is the default and the worst option.

RULE OF THUMB FOR RETRIEVAL-BACKED FEATURES: show the user what was retrieved. It costs interface, it improves trust calibration, and it turns 'the AI was wrong' into 'it looked at the wrong document' — which is a debuggable, fixable, and far less trust-destroying failure.

title: Reasoning Structure — When to Ask for Steps
content:
Asking a model to reason before answering improves accuracy on multi-step problems and costs latency and tokens. It is a trade-off with a UX dimension.

WHEN STRUCTURED REASONING HELPS: arithmetic and quantitative work, multi-constraint problems, anything requiring the model to check its own work, classification against fine-grained criteria, and planning before acting.

WHEN IT DOES NOT: simple retrieval, formatting, rewriting, and anything where latency dominates the user's experience of quality.

THE UX DECISIONS THAT COME WITH IT:
- SHOW OR HIDE? Hidden reasoning means a longer wait with nothing to look at. Shown reasoning turns dead time into legible progress and improves trust calibration. Shown-but-collapsed is usually the right default.
- SUMMARISE, DO NOT DUMP. Full reasoning traces are noise for most users. A three-line summary of the approach is signal. Keep the full trace available for the users who want it.
- SEPARATE REASONING FROM ANSWER visually and structurally, so the answer can be copied without the working.
- ANSWER-FIRST OUTPUT ORDER even when reasoning happened first. The user wants the conclusion at the top; the reasoning is support. This is a formatting constraint (pa-003), and it is frequently violated by default.

THE PLAN-THEN-ACT PATTERN for agentic features: have the system produce a plan, show it to the user, let them adjust it, then execute. This is a reasoning structure and a human-in-the-loop checkpoint at once, and it is the cheapest way to make an agentic feature feel controllable rather than unpredictable.

WHAT TO AVOID: exposing raw chain-of-thought as the primary output; making the user read the reasoning to find the answer; and using visible reasoning as a substitute for actually reducing latency.

title: Prompt Versioning and Change Management
content:
A prompt is production code that determines the product's voice and quality. Treat it accordingly.

WHAT TO VERSION:
- The prompt text itself, in source control.
- The model and its version, since the same prompt behaves differently across models.
- The example set.
- The evaluation rubric and the regression set results at that version.
- Any tool definitions and their schemas.

THE CHANGE PROCESS:
1. State what you are trying to change, behaviourally. 'Reduce average response length' or 'stop offering further help at the end', not 'improve tone'.
2. Run the regression set BEFORE. Without a baseline you cannot tell improvement from change.
3. Make one change.
4. Run the regression set after. Look specifically at areas you did NOT intend to affect, because that is where the surprise lives.
5. Record the diff, the intent, and the measured effect.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN IT SOUNDS: prompt edits have non-local effects. Tightening the length constraint can make refusals curt. Adding a hedging rule can make confident answers hedge. Adding an example can shift the format of unrelated task types. Without a regression set, these regressions ship and are attributed to 'the model changed'.

WHAT DESIGN SHOULD INSIST ON:
- A named owner for the prompt, the way a component has an owner.
- Design review on changes affecting voice, format, length, or refusal behaviour.
- The regression set includes the persona's hard cases (ab-003) — not knowing, being wrong, being pushed back on, refusing.
- A rollback path, and a record of what the previous version did.

A PROMPT WITH NO REGRESSION SET IS AN UNTESTED INTERFACE. It will drift, and the drift will be discovered by users.
